headline: High risk: shared filesystem and broad tool access make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A reads and writes local files and exposes stdin/stdout and API surfaces; Agent B shares state via filesystem and can use MCP/browser tools. That creates a plausible default bridge where A’s content can be consumed by B as instructions, even without a documented direct channel. Both profiles support the pathway.
conditions: IF Agent A writes attacker-controlled text into a workspace file that Agent B later reads
IF Agent B ingests file contents or MCP output without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a provenance banner to all inter-agent files
Restrict B to read-only review of A outputs
Use separate workspaces for A and B
Disable MCP for B during handoff
requires-engineering: add content-signing or trust labels

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A handles configuration secrets and academic papers, while Agent B has broad network egress and workspace sharing via filesystem. In default use, A’s files can reach B, and B can transmit them externally. That makes exfiltration of sensitive material plausible without special setup; uncertainty favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF Agent A stores secrets or sensitive paper data in the shared workspace
IF Agent B reads those files and sends context to a remote model API or MCP server
mitigations: Separate secret-bearing files from the shared workspace
Rotate or stub secrets before joint runs
Disable B network egress for handoff sessions
Use per-agent workspaces with explicit copy steps
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction on file transfer

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, execute shells, and spawn subprocesses; B also modifies git state and shares state via filesystem. On a shared workspace, concurrent edits and repo mutations can collide and corrupt work products. A lacks git writes, but B’s broader mutation surface still makes the pair dangerous by default.
conditions: IF A and B operate in the same directory or repo
IF B commits or rewrites files while A is still producing outputs
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes
Turn off B git mutations during A runs
Use file locks for shared artifacts
requires-engineering: add workspace-level transaction/locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces content-writing and RAG outputs, and B can act on workspace files and browser/MCP results. If B treats A’s generated text as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or code changes. The pairwise pathway is plausible in default workflows, but B’s approval-per-tool action reduces the blast radius somewhat.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as source material for code, browser actions, or MCP calls
IF no verification step checks A’s claims before B acts
mitigations: Require B to cite source files before acting
Add a verification checklist between agents
Limit B to read-only summarization of A outputs
Mark A outputs as untrusted drafts
requires-engineering: add automated fact-check gates

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly handles configuration secrets and research data, while B handles source code and browser screenshots under broad network egress. The profiles do not document residency or retention mismatches, but they do show different data classes and logging surfaces that can create retention or disclosure gaps when combined. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated or confidential data from A is copied into B’s workspace
IF B’s screenshots or logs retain that data beyond the intended retention window
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in B’s workspace
Redact secrets before transfer
Set short log retention for both tools
Document data-class handling rules for the pair
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls
